title: Short Stuff: Yakhchāls - Ancient Fridges
summary: Short Stuff episode on yakhchāls (Persian ice houses/ancient refrigerators). The hosts cover their origins in ancient Persia (at least as old as 400 BC, in modern Iran and parts of Afghanistan and Tajikistan), the sand-clay-egg white-lime-goat hair-ash insulating mortar called sarouj, and a 2018 Max Fordham engineering analysis of their insulating properties. They explain how ice was made by diverting water from qanats into shaded shallow pits to freeze in layers overnight, aided by the conical dome shape (solar chimney effect) and wind catchers called badgirs. They discuss using the ice to store food and make the dessert faloodeh, selling ice at market, radiative cooling on clear low-humidity nights, the decline of yakhchāls due to modern refrigeration and dust contamination, the surviving example in Kerman, and interest in preserving them for passive cooling.

segments.title: Pronouncing yakhchāl
segments.summary: The hosts banter about how to pronounce 'yakhchāl' and agree to each use their own pronunciation.

segments.title: Ancient Persian ice refrigerators
segments.summary: Chuck introduces yakhchāls as ancient cooling systems found across ancient Persia, at least as old as 400 BC, in modern Iran, and still present in Iran, Afghanistan and Tajikistan. Their fridge name is noted, and their freezing of ice in a hot climate is described as puzzling.

segments.title: Sarouj insulating mortar
segments.summary: The hosts describe the insulation of yakhchāl walls, made from a mortar called sarouj of sand, clay, egg whites, lime, goat hair and ash. A 2018 Max Fordham analysis found the walls insulated as well as three inches of concrete wrapped in a foot of styrofoam.

segments.title: How ice was made in winter
segments.summary: Water was diverted from underground channels called qanats into shallow shaded pits or ponds on the north side of tall walls, where it froze in layers over several nights. Once ice reached about fifty centimeters it was cut into blocks and stored through the summer.

segments.title: Conical dome and wind catchers
segments.summary: The conical dome is said to optimize the solar chimney effect, drawing warm air up and out through a top opening. Wind catchers called badgirs direct wind downward into the dome, where air is cooled by the ice and rises out.

segments.title: Uses for the ice and faloodeh
segments.summary: The ice was used to keep food cold and to make faloodeh, a Persian frozen dessert of vermicelli noodles, semi-frozen rose-water sugar syrup, lime juice and ground pistachios. The hosts joke about the pistachios.

segments.title: Public access, radiative cooling and ice trade
segments.summary: The Kerman yakhchāl is about five stories tall, and yakhchāls were open to the public and also built for private homes. Ice and sorbets were sold at market by donkey. Clear, dry nights let heat escape, helping thin ice layers form. A Max Fordham estimate put output at about three million ice cubes a season.

segments.title: Decline and preservation
segments.summary: Yakhchāls declined with modern refrigeration and because ice made in the open was contaminated with dust. Groups in Kerman are working to restore some for museum and tourism purposes to preserve the culture.

segments.title: Lessons for passive cooling
segments.summary: Josh says yakhchāls offer lessons for passive cooling methods that use less energy, and the hosts make jokes closing the topic.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the Short Stuff episode.

segments.title: Production credit
segments.summary: Closing credit noting Stuff You Should Know is an iHeartRadio production.
